title: Modeling and solving the crew rostering problem
contribution: A looped-cycle multigraph model of railway crew rostering whose Lagrangian bound reduces to two assignment problems, with the multipliers fixed by the 1440-minute structure of the arc lengths, and a one-roster-at-a-time construction steered by the AP reduced costs with bound-guided refinement; the code won FS's FARO competition and reaches the weeks bound on 26 of 36 test instances by the authors' count.
problem_entry: An FS/AIRO competition (FARO: three instances up to 1,000 duties, 90 minutes on a PC 486/33, codes run by FS) and a difference of objective: earlier rostering work balanced workload in urban transit, railway rostering minimises crews under involved sequencing rules (pp. 2–3).
key_idea: Encode the sequencing rules in a multigraph with three arc types and idle-day loops, drop the infeasible-path constraints and relax two counting constraints so that the bound is one AP (Proposition 1); fix the multipliers at 1440/1440 or 1440/0 instead of running subgradient; score each construction move by AP reduced costs and the parametric bound increase, then remove and rebuild every roster whose imposition raises the bound (pp. 6–16).
assumptions: Periodic CRP with k-day weeks whose k-th day is idle, rosters as cyclic week sequences, objective total weeks (crews = k x weeks); ILP with arc and loop binaries and constraints for every minimal infeasible looped path, left unstrengthened by choice; redundant w, z constraints added for the relaxation; FARO rules (k = 6, q = 60, weekly caps, at least 40% double rests, 170 paid hours per 30 days, 36 working hours per 7 days, a special roster, a hierarchical objective); 8 instances of 21–525 duties (pp. 4–10, 16–19, 23).
proof_devices: Proposition 1: per vertex pair keep the arc of minimum Lagrangian cost, solve one AP, then take the smallest integer w satisfying (16) and z = ceil(beta w); O(n^3), p. 12
validity of the replacement inequality (15) by comparing its right-hand side with that of (9), p. 11
multipliers fixed by the lattice structure of the arc lengths (multiples of 1440): two APs replace subgradient optimisation, pp. 12–13

lexicographic bounds valid only if every higher-level bound equals its optimal value; epsilon added to arcs that need a technical interval; a dummy duty forcing the special roster; combinations (18)–(19), pp. 20–21
trivial O(n) bounds from each attribute cap, pp. 11, 19
experiments: FARO as run by FS: seven teams, three with valid solutions on all instances; the authors' code 48/112/165 weeks against bounds 48/108/164, rivals 48–49/113/168, under one 90-minute limit (Table 1, p. 22); the improved post-competition version on 36 instances (8 FARO plus 28 merged pairs), 60/150 minutes on a Pentium 90, with 26/36 claimed tight and a 0.8% mean gap (pp. 23–25); my reading of Table 3: 25 within the stated limits plus F69F525 from a 300-minute run, the text's F164F525 a slip; no rival on the merged set; single runs, no seeds.
positioning: Prior rostering, airline set-partitioning and cyclic-scheduling work set aside by its objective in one paragraph (p. 3); the competing teams named and their reports cited (p. 22); the model presented as general for airline and railway rostering (p. 4).
writing: Abstract in the order gap, relaxation, bound-driven heuristic, results, competition win (p. 2); design choices backed by 'computational experience' rather than shown experiments (pp. 12–13); the general model kept apart from the FARO rules (pp. 16–21); no conclusions section (p. 24).
limits_future: The LP-strengthening route is left unexplored (p. 9); the bound is weak where paid time binds (FARO360, p. 22); no future work stated.

title: A heuristic method for the set covering problem
contribution: A three-phase Lagrangian heuristic for very large set covering (subgradient with a new step rule and small-norm directions, a Lagrangian-score greedy at many near-optimal multipliers, column fixing), run on a dynamically priced core and followed by gap-share refinement; it won FS's FASTER competition and matched or beat the published heuristics on the OR Library and on airline and bus instances.
problem_entry: FS crew-scheduling SCPs up to 5,000 rows and 1,000,000 columns that the classical approaches handle badly, posed as the FASTER competition (undisclosed instances, fixed machines and limits, codes run by FS) (pp. 1–2); exact codes stop at a few hundred rows and a few thousand columns (p. 3).
key_idea: Near-equivalent multipliers give very different solutions and the bound does not predict solution quality, so explore many near-optimal multipliers with a Lagrangian-score greedy, restart from randomly perturbed multipliers, fix good columns and recurse; counter dual degeneracy with a step rule driven by the bound's spread and a small-norm direction from a prime cover; keep the core dynamic by Lagrangian pricing; refine by fixing the incumbent columns with the smallest gap shares (pp. 5–15).
assumptions: Pure SCP with positive integer costs; the integrality property of the Lagrangian subproblem; massive dual degeneracy in crew-scheduling instances (over 1,000 near-zero Lagrangian costs per iteration on RAIL516); no preprocessing of dominated rows and columns, by design; no optimality proof; FASTER costs 1–2 with at most 12 rows per column, OR-Library costs 1–100, airline costs up to 7 digits (pp. 3–4, 7, 16–18, 23).
proof_devices: integrality property: optimal LP duals solve the Lagrangian dual, p. 4
small-norm direction from a prime partial cover of the near-zero-cost columns, no longer guaranteed to be a subgradient, pp. 7–8
step-size rule from the best and worst bounds over p = 20 iterations (halve if more than 1% apart, multiply by 1.5 if within 0.1%), p. 7
a valid lower bound exists only after pricing; pricing interval T adapted to the relative bound change at pricing, p. 13
exact duality-gap identity splitting the gap into column terms and over-cover row terms, giving per-column gap shares delta_j (9) used to choose fixings, p. 14
experiments: FASTER samples against the Roma group and the best commercial package, and the competition against every group FS ran (best on all three instances) (pp. 17–18); equal-time ablation of column fixing (Table 1, p. 12) and single-instance plots of the step and direction rules (pp. 7–9); OR-Library, Wedelin and Balas–Carrera sets at 5,000 s on a DECstation 5000/240 against five heuristics with converted times and per-rival time rules (pp. 18–24); CPLEX 3.0 runs up to 600,000 s as referee (p. 21); the claimed 92 of 94 optimal or best known becomes at most 91 by my count (SASjump above the CPLEX optimum, p. 24), with two sample values only from ad hoc tuning (p. 17); single runs, no seeds.
positioning: In the Balas–Ho Lagrangian line, crediting Fisher and Kedia (Lagrangian costs in a greedy), Ceria, Nobili and Sassano (variable fixing, static core) and Carraresi and Gallo (Lagrangian relaxation with column generation); novelty claimed 'to our knowledge' for pricing with Lagrangian relaxation in SCP (pp. 4, 10–12, 17).
writing: Application and competition first in the abstract; design choices backed by 'computational experience' and single-instance convergence plots; a strong closing claim that no comparable commercial or academic code is known, and a generalisation to 0-1 programs conditional on a replacement for GREEDY (pp. 1, 5–13, 24–25).
limits_future: No optimality proof (p. 18); three refinement parameters called very important with no sensitivity shown (p. 15); future work on the base constraints of railway crew scheduling and on other 0-1 linear programs (pp. 24–25).

title: Algorithms for the set covering problem
contribution: A computational survey of set covering algorithms on the OR Library (classes A–H) in which the authors' heuristic gives the best known value on all instances, their LP code runs almost 5 times faster than tuned CPLEX 4.0.8, and general-purpose ILP solvers (CPLEX 4.0.8, MINTO 2.3) beat the special-purpose exact codes, more so when fed the authors' preprocessing.
problem_entry: A survey of recent effective heuristic and exact SCP methods restricted to those tested on Beasley's OR Library, with the easy classes 4, 5, 6 and e dropped by a stated rule (pp. 1–2).
key_idea: The effective SCP methods solve the LP dual heuristically through Lagrangian or surrogate substitutes; relaxations used in heuristics are compared by the heuristics they drive, not by their bounds; exact codes are compared with general-purpose ILP solvers, plain and with an external preprocessing (pp. 2–9).
assumptions: SCP with positive integer costs; the integrality property makes LP and Lagrangian duals coincide; reduction rules exist but each algorithm's preprocessing is omitted; OR-Library classes A–H from 300 x 3,000 to 1,000 x 10,000, densities 2–20%, costs 1–100 (pp. 1–3, 12).
proof_devices: Lagrangian cost fixing in both directions against the incumbent (fix to 0 if L(u) + c_j(u) >= UB, to 1 if L(u) - c_j(u) >= UB), p. 4
partial relaxation that keeps a set of disjoint rows: its best bound equals the LP value, p. 4
greedy repair of any multiplier vector into a dual feasible one without lowering the bound, p. 3
explanatory argument: bounds stronger than the LP are hard to get cheaply, hence LP-based branch-and-bound and general-purpose ILP codes are competitive, p. 8
experiments: Table 1: the authors' LP code at about 10 s (7 s of it in CPLEX calls) against CPLEX 4.0.8 primal, dual, network and barrier, each tuned on the 40 instances (about 420, 46, 46 and 370 s) (pp. 5, 12); Tables 2–4, absent from this copy, summarised in the prose: heuristic quality and times (pp. 7–8), exact codes at 1,500–3,000 s against CPLEX about 700 and MINTO about 750 s, about 400 and 500 s with the external preprocessing (p. 9); times converted to a DECstation 5000/240 by a stated crude approximation (p. 2); one number per source, no variability.
positioning: History deferred to Balas's survey and the Ceria–Nobili–Sassano bibliography; each method described in its authors' terms, unspecified details in rivals' papers named, unfair comparisons declined; the authors' own codes are in every comparison and best or tied (pp. 1, 5–8).
writing: Relaxations, then heuristics, then exact methods, each ending in a comparison; explicit hedges ('apparently', 'According to our opinion'); no conclusions, the paper ending on the measured sentence about general-purpose ILP solvers (pp. 2, 5, 8–9).
limits_future: Rival times converted roughly; several comparisons impossible; no future work stated (pp. 2, 8).

title: Solving the asymmetric travelling salesman problem with time windows by branch-and-cut
contribution: A computational comparison of three ATSP-TW formulations (big-M arrival times, arc variables with infeasible-path constraints, arc-time variables) on real stacker-crane instances, in which the arc-only model wins 16 of 22 runs and becomes an ABACUS branch-and-cut with preprocessing, LP-based heuristics and many cut families that solves real instances up to 127 nodes.
problem_entry: A Siemens Nixdorf stacker-crane application that needs offline ATSP-TW optima to judge online heuristics, and an open formulation choice: no natural IP model and no way to know which computes best, so computational experience decides (p. 3); the literature has no benchmarks and only random data (p. 4).
key_idea: Implement Model 1 (MTZ big-M with arrival times), Model 2 (arc variables only, infeasible-path elimination) and Model 3 (arc-time variables), whose arc projections coincide, on equal footing; harvest cuts from the ATSP, SOP and one-machine scheduling relaxations; choose the winner by measurement and build an advanced code for it (pp. 6–13, 22–23).
assumptions: ATSP-TW with nonnegative integer data, infinite due dates allowed, waiting allowed, the triangle inequality on processing-plus-travel times; feasibility strongly NP-complete and path feasibility NP-complete, hence checkable sufficient conditions (Lemmas 3.3 and 4.13); SNI instances rbg* up to 233 nodes plus rbg27.b.x with randomly relaxed windows; Model 2 limited to TSP-type objectives (pp. 2–9, 22, 26, 32).
proof_devices: Lemma 3.3: sufficient conditions for path infeasibility (a violated deadline, or a node that no extension of the path can cover), pp. 5–6
Lemma 4.13: checkable sufficient conditions for the validity of the strengthened infeasible-path inequalities (4.10)–(4.12), pp. 8–9
projection argument: the arc projections of Models 1 and 3 are Model 2's polytope, p. 8
global-validity invariant: time windows updated only on global fixings, never on local settings, so window-based cuts stay valid in the whole tree, p. 21
tournament-constraint separation by enumerating the polynomially many candidate paths (Savelsbergh), p. 19
strengthened (pi, sigma) separation by a max-flow on a pruned support graph, pp. 19–20
experiments: Eleven instances all three models solved, two run sets (from scratch and with the optimum supplied), the same LP solver (CPLEX 4.09), machine (SPARC Station 10) and depth-first search: Model 2 fastest in 16 of 22 runs, Model 3 winning 6 with few windows (pp. 22–24); the advanced ABACUS code on 50 instances with 5 CPU hours each: 32 solved, largest solved 127 nodes, smallest unsolved 43, cuts per separator call and time shares reported (pp. 26–31); an unremarked slowdown on rbg27.b.04 when the optimum is supplied (p. 24); single runs, no seeds.
positioning: Against dynamic programming and enumeration for the TSP-TW and against random-data studies (p. 4); continues the authors' polyhedral companion paper and Fischetti's ATSP and SOP polyhedral work; credits Maffioli and Sciomachen, van Eijl, Desrochers and Laporte, Savelsbergh (pp. 7–12, 19).
writing: The abstract opens on the model-choice observation and hedges 'at least for our special application'; implementation details get their own section; the conclusion concedes that the polyhedral approach is not the unchallenged winner and lays the numerical trouble on the models, not the software (pp. 2, 18–22, 32).
limits_future: Model 2 cannot handle makespan objectives; instance difficulty is unpredictable; dynamic programming may win with tight windows; future work is very time-consuming implementation to locate each method's advantage (pp. 26, 32).
